newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland, February 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland, February 24.

text.p: The following are the highlights of stories in the Irish press on Monday.

- The chief state solicitor's office "is a seriously under-resourced organisation and is not in a position to efficiently meet the demands placed on it", according to a confidential consultant's report.
- Nearly 100 senior managers in the state-run Telecom Eireann are being asked to apply for new positions within the company on a personal contract basis.
- Scientists in Scotland have created the first clone of an adult animal.
- After a steady decrease every year over the previous five years, the number of cot deaths rose in 1996.
- Real progress in the talks could be made if the Republican movement accepted the fundamental principal of consent, Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said at the weekend.
- By the time divorce becomes law this Thursday, 1,000 people will have registered with the Legal Aid Board seeking a divorce.
- The Irish government is proposing an important amendment to the Working Time Bill and a mechanism to monitor its initial impact.
- The Irish Prime Minister on Sunday night effectively began the general election campaign when he set out the framework of his party's manifesto.
- It will be possible for some couples to get a divorce for as little as 23 Irish pounds when it becomes law later this week.
- In a landmark ruling, the Irish Dental Council has declared that a HIV positive dentist is fit to practise.
- A 60 million Irish pound job-cutting scheme which gets under way at Telecom Eireann this week is designed to cut the company's 11,500 workforce by ten percent.
- The crisis-hit Irish fishing industry is losing an estimated nine million Irish pounds a week as the national fleet faces being tied up for a fourth successive week.

- The Irish government's bill for buying industrial peace among key hospital staff will reach at least 121 million Irish pounds this year following Health Minister Michael Noonan's decision to dampen anger among consultants.
